questions.q: In which year did Confederation create the Dominion of Canada?
questions.explain: Confederation took effect on July 1, 1867, when the British North America Act, a law of the British Parliament, brought the Dominion of Canada into being. Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were the four founding provinces, and the anniversary is marked every year as Canada Day.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is the capital city of Canada?
questions.explain: Queen Victoria picked Ottawa, a city on the Ottawa River in Ontario, as the capital in 1857. Around it, the National Capital Region protects both the historic buildings and the natural setting of the area.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: How many provinces and territories does Canada have?
questions.explain: Canada is made up of ten provinces plus three territories: Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut. Every one of them has a capital, and newcomers should be able to name the capital of their own province or territory, along with Ottawa.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In which year was the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms entrenched in the Constitution?
questions.explain: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms was written into the Constitution in 1982. Since it now forms part of the supreme law, every government in Canada and every law it passes has to respect the rights and freedoms it lists.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

questions.q: Who are the three founding peoples of Canada usually named in the study guide?
questions.explain: The guide describes Canada as built on three founding peoples: Aboriginal peoples, who were here first, and the French and British, whose settlers brought the languages, laws and institutions that shaped the country.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is the title of Canada's national anthem?
questions.explain: O Canada was proclaimed Canada's national anthem in 1980. English and French Canadians sing different words to the same music, and the anthem is heard at public ceremonies, sporting events and citizenship ceremonies.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which First World War battle did the Canadian Corps win in April 1917?
questions.explain: In April 1917 the Canadian Corps captured Vimy Ridge in France, at a cost of about 10,000 killed or wounded. The victory earned Canadian soldiers a reputation for valour, and April 9 is remembered as Vimy Day.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: The First World War

questions.q: Under the fixed-date election law, how often are federal general elections normally held?
questions.explain: Federal law sets a general election four years after the previous one. This gives voters and parties a predictable calendar, although a government that loses the confidence of the House of Commons can face an earlier vote.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Canadian freedoms draw on a tradition of ordered liberty that goes back to which document, signed in England in 1215?
questions.explain: Magna Carta, also called the Great Charter of Freedoms, was signed in England in 1215. Canadians inherited the tradition it began, which includes freedom of conscience and religion, freedom of expression, and freedom of peaceful assembly and association.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Magna Carta

questions.q: What does habeas corpus protect?
options: The right to vote in secret
The right to a free lawyer in every case
The right to contest being held unlawfully by the state
questions.explain: Habeas corpus comes from English common law. It lets a person who is held by the authorities ask a court to decide whether the detention is lawful, so that nobody can be imprisoned arbitrarily.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Habeas corpus

questions.q: Which pair are both sources of Canadian law?
options: English common law and the civil code of France
The U.S. Constitution and Spanish colonial law
The Hudson's Bay Company charter and church law
Roman military law and Dutch merchant law
questions.explain: Canadian law draws on several roots: laws adopted by Parliament and by the provincial legislatures, the common law of England, France's civil code, and the unwritten constitutional customs that Canada received from Great Britain.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Sources of Canadian law

questions.q: Under the Charter's mobility rights, Canadians can:
options: Settle in any other country without a visa
Vote in any province they happen to visit
Live and work anywhere in Canada and enter or leave the country freely
Stop paying provincial taxes when they move
questions.explain: Mobility rights let citizens move to and take jobs in any province or territory, leave Canada and come back, and apply for a passport. They are among the most important rights set out in the Charter.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Mobility rights

questions.q: Which of these is a fundamental freedom that Canadians enjoy?
options: Freedom to ignore a jury summons
questions.explain: Canada's fundamental freedoms include freedom of conscience and religion; of thought, belief, opinion and expression; of peaceful assembly; and of association. They protect people who meet, demonstrate or organize without violence.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Fundamental freedoms

questions.q: If you are called to serve on a jury in Canada, what does the law say?
options: You are legally required to serve
You must pay a fee in order to serve
You may refuse without giving a reason
questions.explain: Jury service is both a privilege and a legal duty. Courts rely on impartial juries made up of ordinary citizens, so a person who is summoned must take part unless legally excused.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Citizenship responsibilities

questions.q: Is military service compulsory in Canada?
options: Yes, for all citizens aged 18 to 25
No, there is no compulsory military service
Yes, for one year after becoming a citizen
questions.explain: Canada has no compulsory military service. Joining the regular Canadian Forces or the part-time reserves is voluntary and is presented as an honourable way to serve the country and an excellent career choice.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Defending Canada

questions.q: What does the rule of law mean in Canada?
options: Police may act without legal limits
The Prime Minister can overrule any court
Everyone, including leaders and officials, must obey the law
Each community writes its own criminal code
questions.explain: The rule of law is one of Canada's founding principles. Individuals and governments alike are governed by laws rather than by arbitrary decisions, and obeying the law is a basic responsibility of every citizen.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Citizenship responsibilities

questions.q: The Charter of Rights and Freedoms opens by stating that Canada is founded upon principles that recognize what?
options: The equality of all political parties
The rule of law and the supremacy of God
The primacy of the English language
The authority of the provinces over Parliament
questions.explain: The Charter begins by recognizing two founding principles: the rule of law and the supremacy of God. These first words reflect the place of religious traditions in Canada and the respect owed to the dignity and worth of each person.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

questions.q: How are women and men treated under Canadian law?
options: Women need a guardian to sign contracts
Equality applies only in some provinces
They are equal under the law
questions.explain: Women and men have the same legal standing in Canada, in the family, at work and in public life. Canada's openness to other cultures does not extend to any practice that denies this equality.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: The Equality of Women and Men

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a responsibility of Canadian citizens?
questions.explain: Citizens have a duty to limit waste and pollution and to protect Canada's natural, cultural and architectural heritage so that it can be passed on. Obeying the law, serving on a jury when called and voting are other responsibilities.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Citizenship responsibilities

questions.q: Which program lets young Canadians learn discipline, responsibility and skills in a military-style setting?
questions.explain: The guide encourages young people to join the cadets, which teach discipline, responsibility and practical skills. Adults can serve in the regular forces or in the part-time navy, militia and air reserves.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: Defending Canada

questions.q: According to the Charter, what is the status of English and French in Parliament and the federal government?
options: French is used only in Quebec
questions.explain: Two kinds of language rights are protected by the Charter: the rights attached to the official languages and the right to be educated in the minority official language. In Parliament and across the federal government, English and French stand on an equal footing.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

questions.q: How does the Charter treat the treaty rights of Aboriginal peoples?
options: It applies only to First Nations living on reserve
Charter rights do not take away from Aboriginal treaty and other rights
questions.explain: According to the Charter, the rights it guarantees cannot be used to weaken the treaty rights or any other rights and freedoms held by Aboriginal peoples. The Constitution also recognizes Aboriginal and treaty rights in a separate provision.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Rights and Responsibilities of Citizenship: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

questions.q: Who are the Métis?
options: An Inuit community of the eastern Arctic
A distinct people with both Aboriginal and European ancestors
The first French settlers of Acadia
questions.explain: The Métis are a people in their own right, descended from both Aboriginal and European ancestors. Some of their communities are French-speaking and others English-speaking, and they are one of the three groups covered today by the term Aboriginal peoples.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which phrase from the British North America Act of 1867 sums up the commitment of Canada's institutions?
options: Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
questions.explain: The phrase peace, order and good government comes from the British North America Act of 1867, the founding constitutional text. Canadian institutions remain attached to it, as they are to liberty within the law, enterprise, hard work and fairness.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which document of 1763 first guaranteed the territorial rights of Aboriginal peoples?
options: The Royal Proclamation issued by King George III
questions.explain: The Royal Proclamation of 1763, issued by King George III, first guaranteed Aboriginal territorial rights and laid the basis for negotiating treaties with newcomers. Those treaties were not always fully respected, and Aboriginal and treaty rights are now in the Constitution.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In 2008, the Government of Canada formally apologized to former students of which institutions?
questions.explain: From the 1800s to the 1980s, many Aboriginal children were placed in residential schools meant to assimilate them. The schools were poorly funded, students suffered hardship and abuse, and their languages and cultures were mostly banned. Ottawa formally apologized in 2008.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which three distinct groups make up the Aboriginal peoples of Canada?
questions.explain: The term Aboriginal peoples covers three distinct groups: First Nations, the Inuit of the Arctic, and the Métis. Each group has its own history, cultures and rights, which are recognized in the Constitution.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What does the word Inuit mean in the Inuktitut language?
questions.explain: In Inuktitut, the word Inuit means the people. Inuit communities are small and spread out across the Arctic, and a deep understanding of the land, the sea and the animals allowed them to live in one of the world's most demanding climates.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which is the only officially bilingual province?
questions.explain: New Brunswick is the only province that is officially bilingual in English and French. About one third of its people live and work in French, many of them Acadians. At the federal level, both languages are official across Canada.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Who We Are: English and French

questions.q: What was the Great Upheaval in the history of the Acadians?
options: A famine caused by failed harvests
Their deportation from their homeland between 1755 and 1763
questions.explain: Between 1755 and 1763, while Britain and France were at war, over two thirds of the Acadian population was expelled from its homeland. The Acadians nonetheless kept their identity, and their culture is still very much alive within French-speaking Canada.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Who We Are: English and French

questions.q: In 2006, what did the House of Commons recognize about the Québécois?
options: That Quebec is an independent country
That Quebec no longer sends members to Parliament
That they are a nation inside a united Canada
That French is Canada's only official language
questions.explain: In 2006 the House of Commons recognized the Québécois as a nation inside a united Canada. Most Quebecers speak French and keep a distinct identity, culture and language rooted in the French settlement of the 1600s and 1700s.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Who We Are: English and French

questions.q: Since the 1970s, where have most immigrants to Canada come from?
questions.explain: Asian countries have been the main source of immigrants to Canada since the 1970s. Newcomers join a population made of many ethnic and religious groups living side by side peacefully, a variety that stands out most in the big cities.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Who We Are: Diversity in Canada

questions.q: What is the largest religious affiliation in Canada?
questions.explain: Catholics are the largest religious group in Canada, ahead of the various Protestant churches. The number of Muslims, Jews, Hindus, Sikhs and followers of other faiths is rising, and so is the number of people who say they have no religion.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Who We Are: Diversity in Canada

questions.q: Where are the ancestors of Aboriginal peoples believed to have come from?
options: Asia, many thousands of years ago
questions.explain: Aboriginal peoples are thought to descend from people who came from Asia many thousands of years ago. Their societies were firmly in place long before the first European explorers, with cultures grounded in their bond with the Creator, the land and each other.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In which province do the majority of Francophones live?
questions.explain: Quebec is home to most Canadians whose mother tongue is French. Large francophone communities also exist in Ontario, New Brunswick and Manitoba, and smaller ones are found in the remaining provinces and in the territories.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Who We Are: English and French

questions.q: With whom has the Canadian state traditionally partnered to provide schools and health care and to resettle refugees?
questions.explain: Governments in Canada have a long history of partnership with religious communities: together they have promoted social welfare, harmony and mutual respect, run schools and hospitals, helped refugees settle, and defended freedom of religion and of conscience.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Who We Are: Diversity in Canada

questions.q: Which early Europeans reached Labrador and Newfoundland about 1,000 years ago?
questions.explain: Vikings who had colonized Greenland reached Labrador and the island of Newfoundland about 1,000 years ago. The remains of their settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows are now a World Heritage Site.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Who was the first explorer to map Canada's Atlantic coast, in 1497?
questions.explain: John Cabot, an Italian who had moved to England, landed in 1497 on Newfoundland or Cape Breton Island and claimed it for the English Crown. He drew the first map of Canada's Atlantic coast, but English settlers only arrived in 1610.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: The name Canada is believed to come from kanata, an Iroquoian word meaning what?
questions.explain: Jacques Cartier crossed the Atlantic three times between 1534 and 1542. Two Aboriginal guides used the Iroquoian word kanata, which means village, in front of him, and maps started to show the name Canada in the 1550s.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: Exploring a River, Naming Canada

questions.q: In 1608, Samuel de Champlain built a fortress at the site of which present-day city?
questions.explain: In 1608 Champlain built a fortress on the site of today's Québec City. The settlers had to cope with a very harsh climate, and Champlain formed alliances with the Algonquin, Montagnais and Huron nations, who had long been at war with the Iroquois.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which company received from King Charles II of England, in 1670, exclusive trading rights over the lands draining into Hudson Bay?
questions.explain: The Hudson's Bay Company received a royal charter in 1670 giving it exclusive trading rights over the Hudson Bay watershed. For the next century it competed with Montreal-based fur traders, both relying on alliances with First Nations.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: Struggle for a Continent

questions.q: Which 1759 battle at Québec City brought France's empire in America to an end?
options: The Battle of the Plains of Abraham
questions.explain: In 1759 British forces defeated the French on the Plains of Abraham at Québec City. The victory ended France's empire in North America, and Britain later renamed the colony the Province of Quebec.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: Struggle for a Continent

questions.q: What did the Quebec Act of 1774 do?
options: It allowed religious freedom for Catholics and restored French civil law
It gave women the right to vote
It abolished slavery in British North America
It created the provinces of Ontario and Quebec
questions.explain: The British Parliament passed the Quebec Act to better govern the French-speaking Catholic majority. It allowed religious freedom for Catholics, let them hold public office and restored French civil law, while keeping British criminal law.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: A Tradition of Accommodation

questions.q: In 1791, the Constitutional Act split the Province of Quebec into which two colonies?
questions.explain: The Constitutional Act of 1791 set up two colonies: Upper Canada, with a largely Loyalist, Protestant, English-speaking population, and Lower Canada, largely Catholic and French-speaking. For the first time, both had legislative assemblies chosen by voters.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: The Beginnings of Democracy

questions.q: Which British North American colony was the first to achieve full responsible government, in 1847-48?
questions.explain: Under responsible government, ministers need the support of a majority of elected representatives and must resign if they lose a confidence vote. Nova Scotia was the first colony to obtain it, in 1847-48, followed by the united Province of Canada in 1848-49.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Who became Canada's first Prime Minister in 1867?
questions.explain: Born in Scotland and a lawyer in Kingston, Ontario, Sir John Alexander Macdonald was one of the Fathers of Confederation and became the first Prime Minister of Canada in 1867. His birthday, January 11, is recognized by Parliament as Sir John A. Macdonald Day.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: Canada's First Prime Minister

questions.q: Who led the Métis in the Red River uprising of 1869-70?
questions.explain: In 1869 Canada acquired the northwest from the Hudson's Bay Company without asking the Métis of Red River. Louis Riel then led an armed rising and took Fort Garry. Many Canadians regard him as a champion of Métis rights and as the father of Manitoba.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: Challenge in the West

questions.q: Which national project was completed in 1885 when the last spike was driven?
questions.explain: British Columbia joined Canada in 1871 on the promise of a railway to the Pacific. The Canadian Pacific Railway was completed on November 7, 1885, when Donald Smith drove the last spike. European and Chinese workers built it.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: A Railway from Sea to Sea

questions.q: Which Normandy beach did Canadian troops capture on D-Day, June 6, 1944?
questions.explain: On D-Day, June 6, 1944, 15,000 Canadian soldiers landed on Juno Beach in Normandy and took it from the German Army, during the Allied invasion of occupied Europe. Roughly one Allied soldier in ten on that day was Canadian, and the Canadian Army later freed the Netherlands.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's History: The Second World War

questions.q: In 1947, oil found in which province launched Canada's modern energy industry?
questions.explain: Alberta's oil strike of 1947 launched Canada's modern energy sector. It happened in the years of record growth after the war, when the Canadian economy ranked among the strongest of the industrialized world.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Modern Canada: Trade and Economic Growth

questions.q: During the Cold War, Canada joined other Western democracies in which military alliance?
options: NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization
questions.explain: After 1945 much of Eastern Europe came under Communist rule directed by the Soviet Union. In response, Canada and other Western democracies founded a military alliance, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO).

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: With which country does Canada share the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD)?
questions.explain: NORAD is a joint command run by Canada and the United States for the aerospace defence of North America. It was created during the Cold War and reflects the close security partnership between the two neighbours.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In the early 1950s, Canada took part in a United Nations operation defending which country?
questions.explain: During the Korean War of 1950-53, Canada served in the United Nations force that defended South Korea; about 500 Canadians were killed and 1,000 wounded. Since then Canadian troops have taken part in many UN peacekeeping missions, in places such as Egypt, Cyprus and Haiti.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What name is given to the period of rapid change in Quebec in the 1960s?
questions.explain: In the 1960s Quebec went through rapid social and political change known as the Quiet Revolution. French-Canadian culture flourished, and many Quebecers began to seek separation from Canada, a question later put to referendums.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which 1969 law guarantees French and English services from the federal government across Canada?
questions.explain: A Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, set up in 1963, led to the Official Languages Act of 1969. The Act guarantees that people can deal with the federal government in English or French anywhere in Canada.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In which two years did Quebec voters reject sovereignty in a referendum?
questions.explain: Quebec voters rejected sovereignty in two provincial referendums, in 1980 and 1995. The question of Quebec's autonomy inside Canada is still widely debated and continues to influence the country.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In which year did Aboriginal people obtain the right to vote in federal elections?
questions.explain: Aboriginal people gained the right to vote in 1960, as Canada became a more open society in the decades after the war. Today every Canadian citizen who is 18 or older on voting day may vote.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Who began the Marathon of Hope in 1980 to raise money for cancer research?
questions.explain: Terry Fox lost his right leg to cancer at 18 and in 1980 set out to run across Canada to raise funds for cancer research. He could not finish and died of the disease, but yearly fundraising runs in his name continue his legacy.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Modern Canada: Arts and Culture in Canada

questions.q: Which sport was invented by the Canadian James Naismith in 1891?
questions.explain: James Naismith, a Canadian, invented basketball in 1891. Canada's sporting history also includes Olympic and Paralympic champions and world-class hockey players, and every province and territory has produced star athletes.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Modern Canada: Arts and Culture in Canada

questions.q: Founded in 1920, which group of artists became famous for painting Canada's rugged wilderness?
questions.explain: The Group of Seven, founded in 1920, developed a painting style to capture Canada's rugged wilderness landscapes. They remain among the best-known names in Canadian visual art, alongside later abstract pioneers such as Jean-Paul Riopelle.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Modern Canada: Arts and Culture in Canada

questions.q: Which treatment for diabetes did Sir Frederick Banting and Charles Best discover?
questions.explain: Insulin, the hormone used to treat diabetes, was discovered by Frederick Banting of Toronto and Charles Best. It has saved millions of lives worldwide and is among the most famous Canadian contributions to medicine.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Modern Canada: Arts and Culture in Canada

questions.q: What did Joseph-Armand Bombardier invent?
questions.explain: Joseph-Armand Bombardier, from Quebec, invented the snowmobile, a light vehicle for travelling over snow. It changed winter travel in rural and northern Canada and is one of the best-known Canadian inventions.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Modern Canada: Great Canadian Discoveries and Inventions

questions.q: Sir Sandford Fleming is credited with inventing what?
options: The world system of standard time zones
questions.explain: Sir Sandford Fleming, a railway engineer, devised the world system of standard time zones. Before standard time, each town kept its own local time, which made railway timetables confusing over long distances.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Modern Canada: Great Canadian Discoveries and Inventions

questions.q: What is the Canadarm?
options: A robotic arm used in space
questions.explain: The Canadarm, developed by SPAR Aerospace and the National Research Council, is a robotic arm used in outer space. Canadian astronauts have used it in space exploration, alongside the Canadian Space Agency created in 1989.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Modern Canada: Great Canadian Discoveries and Inventions

questions.q: Which three terms describe Canada's system of government?
options: Federal state, parliamentary democracy, constitutional monarchy
Federal republic, presidential system, elected monarchy
questions.explain: Canada's government rests on three key features: it is a federal state with several orders of government, a parliamentary democracy in which voters elect representatives, and a constitutional monarchy with a hereditary Sovereign as head of state.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is the British North America Act now called?
options: The Charter of Rights and Freedoms
questions.explain: The British North America Act of 1867 is now known as the Constitution Act, 1867. It defined the respective responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments, which is why it remains central to how Canada is governed.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Federal State

questions.q: Which of these is a federal government responsibility?
questions.explain: Ottawa deals with questions that concern the whole country or other nations: national defence, foreign affairs, trade and communications between provinces, money, navigation, criminal law and citizenship. Education, highways and municipal government are provincial matters.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Federal State

questions.q: Which of these falls under provincial responsibility?
questions.explain: Health, education, municipal government, property and civil rights, and highways fall under provincial responsibility. Each province elects a legislative assembly that makes laws in those fields, in the same way the House of Commons does at the federal level.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Federal State

questions.q: Over which two areas do the federal and provincial governments share jurisdiction?
questions.explain: The Constitution gives both Ottawa and the provinces a role in agriculture and immigration. In these fields of shared jurisdiction, both orders of government can make laws, so they often cooperate through agreements.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Federal State

questions.q: What are the three parts of Canada's Parliament?
options: The Governor General, the Supreme Court and the Senate
The Prime Minister, the Cabinet and the courts
The Sovereign, the Senate and the House of Commons
The House of Commons, the provinces and the territories
questions.explain: Parliament is made up of the Sovereign (the King or Queen), the appointed Senate and the elected House of Commons. A bill needs the approval of all three parts, through votes in both chambers and royal assent, to become law.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Parliamentary Democracy

questions.q: How are senators chosen, and until what age may they serve?
options: They are elected by the House of Commons and serve until 70
The Governor General appoints them on the Prime Minister's advice, and they serve until 75
They are elected by voters for four years
They are appointed by the provinces for life
questions.explain: Senators are not chosen by voters. They are appointed by the Governor General, who acts on the Prime Minister's advice, and they can sit until age 75. Like the House of Commons, the Senate studies and reviews bills.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Parliamentary Democracy

questions.q: Who grants royal assent to a bill on behalf of the Sovereign?
questions.explain: Royal assent is the last step before a bill becomes federal law. The Governor General gives it in the Sovereign's name, once the bill has been adopted by the House of Commons and by the Senate.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Parliamentary Democracy

questions.q: At which stage of the legislative process is a bill studied clause by clause?
questions.explain: At committee stage, members examine each clause of the bill in detail and can propose changes. The bill then moves through the remaining stages in the House of Commons before following a similar process in the Senate.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Making laws

questions.q: Who is Canada's head of state?
options: The Speaker of the House of Commons
questions.explain: The head of state is the Sovereign, who inherits the position and reigns within the limits set by the Constitution. The head of government is the Prime Minister, who actually runs the country, and Canada keeps these two roles clearly separate.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Constitutional Monarchy

questions.q: Who represents the Sovereign in each of the ten provinces?
questions.explain: In each province the Sovereign is represented by a Lieutenant Governor, whose role is similar to that of the Governor General at the federal level. The elected head of each provincial government is the Premier.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Constitutional Monarchy

questions.q: In each of the three territories, who acts as the federal government's representative and has a ceremonial role?
questions.explain: Each territory has a Commissioner who represents the federal government and plays a mostly ceremonial role. The territories also have their own elected assemblies and premiers, much like the provinces.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Constitutional Monarchy

questions.q: What are the three branches of government in Canada?
options: Senate, House of Commons and Cabinet
questions.explain: The executive, the legislature and the courts cooperate, sometimes with a healthy tension between them, to protect the rights and freedoms of Canadians. This balance prevents any one branch of government from holding all the power.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Constitutional Monarchy

questions.q: In Canada's Parliament, what is a bill?
options: A proposal for a new law
questions.explain: A bill is a proposed law. It goes through several readings, debates and a committee study in each chamber of Parliament, and it can be amended along the way before it becomes law.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Parliamentary Democracy

questions.q: What must the government do if it is defeated in a non-confidence vote in the House of Commons?
questions.explain: Cabinet ministers answer to the elected House of Commons and need its confidence to stay in office. When they lose a vote of non-confidence, they have to resign. This principle, called responsible government, keeps the government accountable to the people's representatives.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: How Canadians Govern Themselves: Parliamentary Democracy

questions.q: On which day does the fixed-date election law set federal general elections?
questions.explain: Legislation passed by Parliament sets federal general elections on the third Monday in October, four years after the previous general election. An earlier election can still be held if Parliament is dissolved before that date.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is another name for a federal electoral district?
questions.explain: Canada is divided into electoral districts, also called ridings or constituencies. Each one is a geographical area whose voters elect one member of Parliament to sit in the House of Commons.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which conditions must you meet to vote in a federal election?
options: Be a permanent resident who has lived in Canada for one year
Be a citizen and a member of a political party
Be a Canadian citizen, aged 18 or over on election day, and registered on the voters' list
Be at least 21 and own property
questions.explain: Three conditions apply to vote in a federal election or referendum: Canadian citizenship, an age of 18 or more on election day, and registration on the voters' list. Voting is one of the key privileges of being a citizen.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is Elections Canada?
options: A department controlled by the Prime Minister
A neutral agency of Parliament that runs federal elections
A provincial body that counts municipal votes
questions.explain: Elections Canada is a non-partisan agency of Parliament responsible for federal elections and referendums. It organizes voting, prepares the voters' lists and publishes the results, independently of any political party.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What does the right to a secret ballot mean?
options: Only party members know who the candidates are
No one may watch you vote or force you to reveal how you voted
Voters must keep their registration secret
questions.explain: Canadian law protects the secrecy of the vote. You mark your ballot behind a screen, and no one, including your family, your employer or a union representative, can insist on knowing your choice, although you may share it if you wish.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is a majority government?
options: The governing party won more than half of all votes cast
The governing party has half or more of all Commons seats
questions.explain: A party that wins half or more of all Commons seats forms a majority government. A party with fewer than half the seats forms a minority government and has to rely on the support of other parties.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is the Official Opposition?
options: The opposition party that won the largest number of Commons seats
The party that finished second in the popular vote
All senators who vote against a bill
questions.explain: Parties not in power are opposition parties, whose role is to oppose or try to improve government proposals peacefully. The one with the most seats becomes the Official Opposition, also called the Loyal Opposition.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: If you cannot vote on election day, what can you do?
options: Vote the following week at a post office
Vote at an advance poll or by special ballot
Ask a neighbour to vote for you
questions.explain: Voters who cannot, or prefer not to, vote on election day may use the advance polls or a special ballot. Elections Canada announces the dates and places, so every eligible voter has a chance to take part.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Federal Elections: Voting Procedures During an Election Period

questions.q: How do you mark a federal ballot?
options: Mark an X in the circle beside your chosen candidate
Rank all the candidates in order
Sign the back of the ballot
questions.explain: On a federal ballot you mark an X in the circle beside the candidate of your choice, behind a voting screen. You then fold the ballot and hand it to the poll officials before it goes into the ballot box.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Federal Elections: Voting Procedures During an Election Period

questions.q: What are the laws passed by a municipal council called?
questions.explain: Municipal councils, usually led by a mayor, pass by-laws that apply only within the local community. Municipalities look after services such as streets, garbage collection, firefighting, recreation facilities and public transit.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Federal Elections: Other Levels of Government in Canada

questions.q: In a federal election, who becomes the MP for an electoral district?
options: The candidate who receives the most votes
The candidate chosen by the party leader
The candidate who wins more than 50% in a second round
questions.explain: Voters in each district choose among the candidates and parties. The candidate with the most votes wins the seat, even without an absolute majority, and represents both the district and all Canadians in the House of Commons.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: After an election, who normally invites the leader of the party with the most seats to form the government?
questions.explain: As a rule, the Governor General asks the leader of the party that won the largest number of seats in the House to form the government. That leader then becomes Prime Minister and stays in office for as long as the House keeps its confidence in the government.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is the minimum age for a Canadian citizen to run as a candidate in a federal election?
questions.explain: Every Canadian citizen who is 18 or over can be a candidate in a federal election. A single electoral district often has several candidates, some standing for a political party and others running as independents.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Who selects the ministers who make up the federal Cabinet?
questions.explain: The ministers of the Crown are selected by the Prime Minister, usually from the members of the House of Commons. As the Cabinet, they run the federal departments and take the main decisions on how Canada is governed.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What does the presumption of innocence mean?
options: Everyone is innocent until proven guilty
Police decide guilt before a trial
An accused person must prove their innocence
questions.explain: In criminal cases, Canada's justice system starts from the presumption of innocence: anyone charged with a crime is considered innocent until a court finds them guilty. This is one element of the due process to which everyone is entitled.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is due process?
options: The method used to appoint judges
A fee charged to start a court case
The rule that the state has to respect every legal right a person holds
A rule that every trial must last a set time
questions.explain: Due process means the state must respect every legal right a person has under the law, for example when arresting, charging or trying someone. It is part of a legal heritage that includes the rule of law and democratic principles.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is the highest court in Canada?
options: The Court of Appeal for Ontario
questions.explain: The Supreme Court of Canada is the country's highest court and the final court of appeal. Below it are the Federal Court, provincial appeal and trial courts, and courts that deal with smaller matters.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which court deals with matters concerning the federal government?
questions.explain: The Federal Court of Canada hears cases that involve the federal government, such as disputes about federal laws and decisions of federal bodies. Most other matters go through the provincial court systems.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which court handles civil cases involving small sums of money?
questions.explain: Small claims courts settle civil disputes over modest amounts of money, such as unpaid bills or minor damage, in a simpler and less costly way than higher courts. Provinces also have courts for other lesser matters.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In which two provinces does the RCMP not act as the provincial police?
questions.explain: Ontario and Quebec have their own provincial police forces. In the other provinces and in the three territories, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police serves as the provincial or territorial police, as well as in some municipalities.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which police force enforces federal laws throughout Canada?
questions.explain: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, known as the Mounties, is Canada's national police force. It enforces federal laws everywhere in the country, from the Atlantic to the Arctic, and is one of Canada's best-known symbols. Its roots go back to the North West Mounted Police of 1873.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: If you cannot afford a lawyer, what is usually available in your community?
options: Legal aid services, free or at low cost
A lawyer paid for by the police
questions.explain: A lawyer can advise you on a legal problem and represent you before a court. People who cannot afford one can usually turn to legal aid, offered in most communities for free or at a reduced cost.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: The Justice System: Getting Legal Help

questions.q: To whom do Canada's laws apply?
options: To everyone, judges, politicians and police officers included
questions.explain: No one is above the law in Canada. Laws apply equally to ordinary residents and to those who hold power, such as judges, politicians and police officers, which reflects the principle of the rule of law.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Who makes Canada's laws?
questions.explain: Laws are the written rules meant to guide people in society. In Canada they are made by the representatives that citizens elect to Parliament and to the provincial and territorial legislatures.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In Canada's legal system, what is the main role of the courts?
questions.explain: Canada's legal system divides the work: elected representatives write the laws, judges resolve disputes and the police make sure laws are respected. This division gives society a peaceful way to settle conflicts.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What does the blindfolded figure of Lady Justice symbolize?
options: The impartial way the law is applied
questions.explain: Lady Justice is shown blindfolded to signify that laws are administered impartially, blind to every consideration except the facts. Justice is meant to treat everyone the same, whatever their wealth, origin or status.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In which situation can you ask the police for help?
options: When someone you know has gone missing
questions.explain: The role of the police is to protect people and make sure the law is obeyed. You can call on them after an accident, a theft or an assault, when you witness a crime, or when a person you know has disappeared.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What role do prisons play in Canada's justice system?
questions.explain: Prisons play an essential role in the justice system: they punish people convicted of crimes and help deter others from committing them. A prison sentence follows a court decision made with due process, never an arbitrary act of the state.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Besides the specialized courts, most provinces have which two main levels of court?
options: A municipal court and a royal court
An appeal court and a trial court
A senate court and a jury court
A federal court and a military court
questions.explain: In most provinces there is a trial court and an appeal court that can review its decisions. The trial court goes by different names depending on the province. Provincial courts also deal with lesser offences.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In which year was the current Canadian flag, with the red maple leaf, first raised?
questions.explain: Canada's red and white maple leaf flag flew for the first time in 1965. Since the Middle Ages, red and white had been colours associated with both France and England, and the flag soon became one of the most recognized symbols of the country.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: The red-white-red pattern of the Canadian flag comes from the flag of which institution?
options: The Royal Military College in Kingston
questions.explain: The red, white and red design of the flag is borrowed from the banner of Kingston's Royal Military College, founded in 1876 in Ontario. The college still trains officers for the Canadian Armed Forces, and its colours became a lasting part of the national identity.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What does Canada's motto, A Mari Usque Ad Mare, mean?
questions.explain: The Latin motto A Mari Usque Ad Mare means from sea to sea. It was adopted with Canada's official coat of arms after the First World War as an expression of national pride, echoing a country that stretches across a continent.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canadian Symbols: Coat of Arms and Motto

questions.q: Which trophy, donated by a Governor General in 1892, is the championship of the National Hockey League?
questions.explain: The Stanley Cup was given in 1892 by Lord Stanley, who was Governor General at the time. Hockey took shape in Canada during the 19th century; it is the national winter sport and draws the largest crowds of spectators.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is Canada's official summer sport?
questions.explain: Lacrosse is an ancient sport first played by Aboriginal peoples and is Canada's official summer sport. Hockey holds the matching title for winter, and both games are closely tied to Canadian history and identity.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which animal appears on the Canadian five-cent coin?
questions.explain: The beaver, a hard-working rodent, has been a Canadian emblem for a long time. You can see it on the 5-cent piece, on the provincial arms of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and on the arms of cities such as Montreal and Toronto.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In which year did Canada start its own system of honours by creating the Order of Canada?
questions.explain: Canada relied on British honours for a long time before founding the Order of Canada in 1967, a hundred years after Confederation. Honours reward exceptional citizens, and any person can put forward the name of a fellow citizen who deserves one.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canadian Symbols: The Order of Canada and Other Honours

questions.q: What is the highest honour available to Canadians?
questions.explain: The Victoria Cross rewards exceptional courage, a bold act of valour or self-sacrifice, or outstanding devotion to duty while facing the enemy. It is the highest honour open to Canadians, and close to a hundred of them have received it since 1854.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: The Peace Tower on Parliament Hill was completed in 1927 in memory of what?
questions.explain: The Peace Tower was completed in 1927 to commemorate the First World War. It is the central tower of the Parliament Buildings, whose Gothic Revival style reflects French, English and Aboriginal traditions.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which emblem, used by the French monarchy for over a thousand years, appears on Quebec's flag?
questions.explain: Tradition holds that the French king adopted the lily flower, or fleur-de-lys, in 496; it went on to stand for the French monarchy, New France included. The flag Quebec adopted in 1948 combines a cross with four fleurs-de-lys.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is Canada's official Royal Flag?
questions.explain: The Union Jack, also called the Royal Union Flag, is Canada's official Royal Flag and recalls the country's ties to the Crown. The provinces and territories also have their own flags reflecting their traditions.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: On Remembrance Day, which flower do Canadians wear to honour those who served and died?
questions.explain: On November 11 each year, Canadians honour veterans and the people who died in war. They wear a red poppy and keep a minute of silence at 11 a.m., the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, and the poem In Flanders Fields is often read.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which ice sport was introduced to Canada by Scottish pioneers?
questions.explain: Curling, a game of sliding heavy stones across the ice toward a target, arrived with Scottish pioneers and remains popular across Canada. Ice hockey, by contrast, was developed in Canada itself during the 1800s.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Since when has the maple leaf appeared on Canadian uniforms and insignia?
questions.explain: No Canadian symbol is better known than the maple leaf. French Canadians took it as an emblem in the 1700s, soldiers have worn it on uniforms and badges since the 1850s, and it is engraved on the gravestones of Canada's war dead.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: In which year did Canada enact free trade with the United States?
questions.explain: Canada and the United States put free trade in place in 1988. Trade is the engine of Canada's economic growth, and Canadians could not keep their standard of living without trading with other nations.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What are the three main types of industries in Canada's economy?
options: Service, manufacturing and natural resources industries
questions.explain: The guide groups Canada's economy into service, manufacturing and natural resources industries. Services provide most jobs, manufacturing makes goods for sale at home and abroad, and resources such as forests, fish and minerals shaped the country's history.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's Economy: Three Main Types of Industries

questions.q: What share of working Canadians have jobs in service industries?
questions.explain: Over three quarters of Canadian workers have jobs in the service sector, which covers fields such as transport, education, health care, construction, banking, communications, retail, tourism and public administration. No other sector employs as many people.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's Economy: Three Main Types of Industries

questions.q: Which country is Canada's largest international trading partner?
questions.explain: Canada and the United States are each other's largest trading partner and share one of the biggest bilateral trading relationships in the world. Integrated supply chains link the two economies and compete together with the rest of the world.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which of these is a natural resources industry?
questions.explain: Forestry, fishing, farming, mining and energy are the natural resources industries. They shaped Canada's history, many regions still rely on them, and resource products account for a large part of what the country exports.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's Economy: Three Main Types of Industries

questions.q: Which of these products comes from Canada's manufacturing industries?
questions.explain: Canadian factories produce goods for the home market and for export, for example paper, high-tech equipment, aerospace products, cars, machinery, food and clothing. A large part of these goods is sold to the United States.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's Economy: Three Main Types of Industries

questions.q: Where does the Peace Arch, a symbol of Canada-U.S. friendship, stand?
options: On the border at Blaine, Washington
questions.explain: The Peace Arch sits on the border between Canada and the United States at Blaine, Washington. One of its inscriptions reads children of a common mother; the other reads brethren dwelling together in unity. The monument stands for the close links and common interests of the two neighbours.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: How is the Canada-United States border traditionally described?
options: As the world's longest undefended border
As the world's most heavily guarded border
As a border that can only be crossed by sea
As a border closed to trade
questions.explain: Millions of Canadians and Americans cross the border safely every year. It is traditionally called the world's longest undefended border, and both countries are committed to keeping it safe, secure and efficient for travellers and trade.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Thanks to its huge supply of fresh water, which province is Canada's largest producer of hydro-electricity?
questions.explain: Thanks to its huge reserves of fresh water, Quebec generates more hydro-electricity than any other province. It also uses the resources of the Canadian Shield for forestry, energy and mining, and it stands out in aeronautics and pharmaceuticals.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which province is Canada's largest producer of oil and gas?
questions.explain: No province produces more oil and gas than Alberta, where the northern oil sands have become a major source of energy. This energy wealth makes Alberta one of the engines of the Canadian economy.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which region is known as Canada's industrial and manufacturing heartland?
questions.explain: Central Canada, meaning the urban areas of southern Ontario and Quebec along the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence, is the industrial and manufacturing core of the country. Over half of the population lives there.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which is Canada's largest and busiest port?
questions.explain: The Port of Vancouver is Canada's largest and busiest port and its gateway to the Asia-Pacific region. It handles billions of dollars' worth of goods traded around the world every year.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which city is Canada's main financial centre?
questions.explain: Toronto, the largest city in Canada, is the country's main financial centre. Ontario's diverse population, natural resources and strategic location support an economy in which services and manufacturing produce a large share of Canada's exports.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which institution, founded in 1934, was set up to control the money supply and make the financial system more stable?
questions.explain: In the Great Depression, Canadians wanted a steadier economy and better social protection. The Bank of Canada, a central bank, was founded in 1934 to control the money supply and keep the financial system stable.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: After the Second World War, which agreement helped open up world trade and later became the World Trade Organization?
options: GATT, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
The North American Free Trade Agreement
questions.explain: After the war, the protectionist trade policies of the Depression gave way to agreements such as GATT, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, which later became the World Trade Organization. More open trade contributed to Canada's record postwar prosperity.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's Economy: Trade and Economic Growth

questions.q: By land area, where does Canada rank among the countries of the world?
questions.explain: Canada covers about 10 million square kilometres, making it the second largest country on earth after Russia. Its territory stretches from the Atlantic to the Pacific and north to the Arctic.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which three oceans border Canada?
options: The Arctic, Indian and Southern oceans
The Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic oceans
The Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans
The Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans
questions.explain: Canada is lined by three oceans: the Pacific to the west, the Atlantic to the east and the Arctic to the north. Along its southern edge lies the boundary with the United States.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of Canada's five regions?
questions.explain: Canada is commonly divided into five regions: the Atlantic Provinces, Central Canada, the Prairies, the West Coast and the North. Each region has its own geography, climate and economy.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
ref.section: Canada's Regions: The Regions of Canada

questions.q: What is the capital of British Columbia?
questions.explain: Victoria, on Vancouver Island, is the capital of British Columbia. It is a tourist centre and the headquarters of the navy's Pacific fleet, while Vancouver is the province's largest city and main port.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is the capital of Nunavut?
questions.explain: Iqaluit is Nunavut's capital. Nunavut was carved out of the eastern Northwest Territories in 1999; most of its people are Inuit, and Inuktitut is one of the territory's official languages.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is the capital of Saskatchewan?
questions.explain: The capital of Saskatchewan is Regina. Saskatoon, the biggest city in the province, is where the mining industry has its headquarters and is a major centre of education, research and technology.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What is the capital of New Brunswick?
questions.explain: Fredericton is the historic capital of New Brunswick, a province founded by United Empire Loyalists. Saint John is its largest city, port and manufacturing centre, and the province is Canada's only officially bilingual one.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which is Canada's smallest province?
questions.explain: Prince Edward Island is Canada's smallest province, famous for its beaches, its red earth and its farms, potatoes above all. It is called the birthplace of Confederation, since the discussions that led to the creation of Canada started there.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Where are the world's highest tides found?
questions.explain: The Bay of Fundy, between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, has the highest tides in the world. Nova Scotia's identity is closely tied to the sea through shipbuilding, fisheries and shipping.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Which of the Great Lakes is the largest freshwater lake in the world?
questions.explain: Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area. It is one of the five Great Lakes; four of them lie between Ontario and the United States, while Lake Michigan is entirely in the U.S.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Where is Mount Logan, Canada's highest mountain?
questions.explain: The highest peak in Canada is Mount Logan, in Yukon. It bears the name of Sir William Logan, a geologist born in Montreal who founded the Geological Survey of Canada and is counted among the country's greatest scientists.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: What does the name Nunavut mean in Inuktitut?
questions.explain: Nunavut means our land in Inuktitut. The territory was established in 1999, and its Legislative Assembly chooses the premier and ministers by consensus rather than along party lines. Most of its people are Inuit.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)

questions.q: Why is Canada's North often called the Land of the Midnight Sun?
options: Because the sun never sets at any time of year
Because in summer the sun can shine for up to 24 hours a day
Because it lies close to the equator
Because the northern lights look like a sun
questions.explain: In the northern summer, the sun can stay up for as long as 24 hours, while in winter it vanishes and long periods of darkness follow. Winters in the territories are long and cold, and summers are short and cool.

ref.doc: Discover Canada (facts only, questions written by Radif Partners)
